author: RELEVANT
title: Gen Z Is Reading More, Not Less — and They’re Going Back to Print
summary: The Atlantic put “The Age of Reading Is Over” on its August cover. full_content:
The Atlantic put “The Age of Reading Is Over” on its August cover. Staff writer Rose Horowitch, who wrote the widely shared 2024 essay “The Elite College Students Who Can’t Read Books,” argued that America has become postliterate — that the decline in book reading now cuts across age, gender and education level, and that comprehension and synthesis are going with it.

But two researchers who study that exact question say their own data runs the other way.

Kathi Inman Berens and Rachel Noorda teach publishing at Portland State University and wrote the Cambridge University Press study “How Gen Z Discover and Consume Books,” built on three waves of nationally representative surveys fielded in 2020, 2022 and 2025.

“According to our 2025 data, a growing proportion of Gen Z — 66% — is identifying as readers, up 14 percentage points from 2022,” they wrote.

Print is where the growth is. Sixty-five percent read at least one print book in the previous 12 months, up from 59% in 2022, and print is the format Gen Z says it prefers.

The researchers tie that to something other than nostalgia: “A longing for ‘digital detox’ is a part of why print books are Gen Z’s top preferred reading format.”

Libraries moved the most. About 36% of Gen Zers said they found a book through a librarian, up from 15% in 2022.

The surveys also found that Gen Zers who didn’t visit libraries had higher loneliness scores than those who did.

Horowitch’s case is that the decline cuts across every age group. On the youngest one, the numbers are going up — and they’re going up on paper.
rewritten_title: Gen Z Reads More Than Predicted—and Chooses Paper Over Screens
